newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Scientology Church members on trial in Lyon.
newsitem.headline: French Scientology Church members on trial in Lyon.

text.p: Twenty-three members of the French Church of Scientology went on trial in the central city of Lyon on Monday in a case expected to provide a rare glimpse of the organisation's inner workings.
The trial, expected to last seven days, was triggered by the 1988 suicide of a church follower in the central city of Lyon.

A five-year investigation of his death, opened at the request of his widow, enabled examining magistrate Georges Fenech to carry out an in-depth exploration of the church's beliefs, practices, global structure and finances.

Prosecutors accuse the church of "exploiting the good faith and gullibility of its victims for commercial profit, through pseudo-scientific and paramedical means, to their financial detriment and at their medical and psychological risk".

The defendants are accused of crimes ranging from manslaughter to embezzlement to fraud and complicity. If convicted, they could be sentenced to up to five years in prison and fined as much as five million francs ($1 million).

The religion, founded in 1954 by the late American science-fiction novelist L. Ron Hubbard, claims more than eight million adherents worldwide, including 4,000 in France, according to officials of the French church.
Members include Hollywood film stars Tom Cruise, Nicole Kidman, John Travolta, Kirstie Alley and Lisa Marie Presley.
Followers are recruited largely through personality tests and then offered expensive books and courses of treatment to resolve problems diagnosed in the tests.
Critics including German Family and Youth Affairs Minister Claudia Nolte accuse it of indoctrinating youth and masquerading as a church while being driven largely by economic motives.

Fenech's investigation found the church charged fees of 12,000 francs ($2,400) for a "purification cure", 22,000 francs ($4,400) for an intensive course and 80,000 francs ($16,000) for a week's course in the Caribbean on its yacht Freewinds.
The trial's origins lie in the 1988 suicide of industrial designer and Scientology follower Patrice Vic, aged 30.
The day he killed himself, he had called on his wife, accompanied by church official Jean-Jacques Mazier, to ask her for a loan of 30,000 francs ($6,000) to pay for church courses.

The Lyon appeals court, which gave the go-ahead for the trial, accused the church during the investigation of pressuring followers, potential witnesses and police to withdraw allegations or refuse to participate in the case.
Church of Scientology spokesman Marc Bromberg denounced the trial as "heresy".

"It's the return of the Inquisition," he told reporters. "This is purely a religious matter. All religions have been accused of fraud. There is no proof in this case. There is no fraud in the Church of Scientology."
